summary.text: Encode each configuration by its tail masses, which evolve by adjacent averaging with floor; stabilization is equivalent to positivity of the final relevant tail. At time \(T(n)\), monotonicity and a diagonal estimate make the \((n+1)\)-process stable within two further steps, while stability by time \(T(n)\) would force the \(n\)-process to have stabilized one step earlier, contradicting minimality.

full_proof.text:
We number the cells from left to right by \(0,1,2,\ldots\). A configuration is a finite list
\[
c=(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_{\ell-1})
\]
of nonnegative integers, with trailing zeroes omitted. In one step, a cell of mass \(m\) retains \(\lceil m/2\rceil\) and sends \(\lfloor m/2\rfloor\) to the next cell on its right. Thus, before trailing zeroes are removed, the new masses are
\[
c'_0=\left\lceil\frac{c_0}{2}\right\rceil,
\qquad
c'_i=\left\lfloor\frac{c_{i-1}}2\right\rfloor+
       \left\lceil\frac{c_i}2\right\rceil \quad(i\geq 1),
\]
where masses outside the finite list are understood to be zero. Let \(S_N(t)\) be the configuration obtained after \(t\) steps from the one-cell configuration \([N]\).

We first replace the individual cell masses by tail masses. For a finite configuration \(c\), put
\[
M_k(c)=\sum_{i\geq k}c_i.
\]
(The sum is finite.) Removing trailing zeroes does not change any \(M_k\). Moreover, direct summation of the update rule gives
\[
M_0(c')=M_0(c)
\]
and, for every \(k\geq0\),
\[
M_{k+1}(c')=
\left\lfloor\frac{M_k(c)+M_{k+1}(c)}2\right\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the mass to the right of the boundary between cells \(k-1\) and \(k\) after the update consists of the halves sent rightward across that boundary, together with the retained and received masses farther to the right. Pairing the retained and sent parts of every cell farther right uses
\(\lceil m/2\rceil+\lfloor m/2\rfloor=m\), and yields (1). Equivalently, writing \(M_k(c)=c_k+M_{k+1}(c)\), the parity calculation for the two half-masses gives exactly the displayed floor.

Accordingly define integers \(Q_N(t,k)\) recursively by
\[
Q_N(0,0)=N,\qquad Q_N(0,k+1)=0,
\]
\[
Q_N(t,0)=N,
\qquad
Q_N(t+1,k+1)=
\left\lfloor\frac{Q_N(t,k)+Q_N(t,k+1)}2\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
Induction on \(t\), using (1), proves the fundamental identity
\[
Q_N(t,k)=M_k(S_N(t)) \quad\text{for all }N,t,k. \tag{3}
\]
In particular, \(Q_N(t,0)=N\) expresses conservation of total mass.

We collect several elementary properties of this array. All quantities below are nonnegative integers.

First, it is nonincreasing in the spatial index:
\[
Q_N(t,k+1)\leq Q_N(t,k). \tag{4}
\]
This follows by induction on \(t\). At time zero it is immediate. At the next time, adjacent entries are floors of averages of adjacent pairs at the preceding time; if the preceding row is nonincreasing, then the pair used farther right is coordinatewise no larger than the pair used immediately to its left. At index zero, the same conclusion follows because every entry is at most the total mass \(N\). Thus (4) also gives
\[
Q_N(t,k)\leq N. \tag{5}
\]
If \(N>0\), the inequality away from index zero is strict:
\[
Q_N(t,k+1)<N. \tag{6}
\]
At time zero this is clear. At the next time, (2), (5), and the induction hypothesis show that the average defining an entry at a positive index has one summand at most \(N\) and the other strictly less than \(N\), so its floor is strictly less than \(N\).

Increasing the initial mass cannot decrease an entry:
\[
Q_N(t,k)\leq Q_{N+1}(t,k). \tag{7}
\]
This is another immediate induction from (2), because taking a floor after division by two is monotone in each summand. In fact the increase is at most one:
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,k)\leq Q_N(t,k)+1. \tag{8}
\]
At time zero this is immediate. If it holds for two adjacent entries at time \(t\), their sum for initial mass \(N+1\) is at most the corresponding sum for initial mass \(N\), plus two. Dividing by two and taking floors therefore increases the next entry by at most one. This proves (8) inductively.

The array is also nondecreasing in time at each fixed index:
\[
Q_N(t,k)\leq Q_N(t+1,k). \tag{9}
\]
For \(k=0\) there is equality. For \(k+1\), spatial monotonicity says
\(Q_N(t,k)\geq Q_N(t,k+1)\), so the floor of their average is at least \(Q_N(t,k+1)\). Iterating (9),
\[
Q_N(t,k)\leq Q_N(t+d,k) \quad(d\geq0). \tag{10}
\]

We next need a stronger comparison between the arrays for \(N\) and \(N+1\).

**Diagonal comparison.** If
\[
Q_N(t,k+1)>0,
\]
then
\[
Q_N(t,k+1)+2\leq Q_{N+1}(t,k). \tag{11}
\]

We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time zero the hypothesis at a positive spatial index is impossible. Consider time \(t+1\).

If \(k=0\), write \(x=Q_N(t,1)\). The left side before adding 2 is
\(\lfloor(N+x)/2\rfloor\). Its positivity implies \(N>0\), and (6) gives \(x<N\). Hence
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N+x}{2}\right\rfloor\leq N-1,
\]
while \(Q_{N+1}(t+1,0)=N+1\), proving (11).

Now suppose \(k=j+1\). Put
\[
a=Q_N(t,j+1),\qquad b=Q_N(t,j+2).
\]
The positivity of \(\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor\), together with \(a\geq b\), implies \(a>0\). By the induction hypothesis,
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,j)\geq a+2. \tag{12}
\]
If \(b>0\), a second use of the induction hypothesis gives
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,j+1)\geq b+2.
\]
Averaging these two inequalities and taking floors proves
\[
Q_{N+1}(t+1,j+1)
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor+2,
\]
as required. If \(b=0\), monotonicity in initial mass gives
\(Q_{N+1}(t,j+1)\geq a\). Together with (12), this gives
\[
Q_{N+1}(t+1,j+1)\geq
\left\lfloor\frac{(a+2)+a}{2}\right\rfloor=a+1.
\]
Since \(a>0\), we have \(a+1\geq\lfloor a/2\rfloor+2\), which is exactly the desired bound because \(b=0\). This completes the proof of (11).

We shall also use a positivity comparison in the opposite direction.

**Shift comparison.** If
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,k+1)>0,
\]
then
\[
Q_N(t,k)>0. \tag{13}
\]
This is proved by induction on \(t\). Again the time-zero hypothesis is impossible. At time \(t+1\), positivity of the average in (2) means that the two relevant entries in the preceding row have sum at least two. If
\(Q_{N+1}(t,k+1)>0\), the induction hypothesis gives \(Q_N(t,k)>0\), and then (9) gives \(Q_N(t+1,k)>0\). If instead \(Q_{N+1}(t,k+1)=0\), positivity of the next average forces
\(Q_{N+1}(t,k)\geq2\). By (8), \(Q_N(t,k)\geq1\), and once more (9) gives positivity at time \(t+1\).

A slightly sharper time-shifted form, obtained from the same two-case argument, is
\[
Q_{N+1}(t+1,k+1)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_N(t,k)>0. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, examine the two entries at time \(t\) whose average defines the hypothesis. If the right entry is positive, (13) applies directly. If it is zero, the left entry is at least two, and (8) makes the corresponding entry for initial mass \(N\) positive.

We now characterize stability. Starting from positive mass \(N>0\), every entry appearing in the trimmed finite configuration \(S_N(t)\) is positive. This follows by induction over the updates: the first updated cell retains \(\lceil m/2\rceil>0\) from a positive first mass, and each subsequent nontrailing entry is a sum of nonnegative half-masses; only a possible terminal zero is removed. Also, by (3) at \(k=0\), the sum of all entries is always \(N\).

It follows that
\[
S_N(t)=(1,1,\ldots,1)\text{ (with \(N\) entries)}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
Q_N(t,N-1)>0. \tag{15}
\]
For the forward implication, the tail beginning at cell \(N-1\) has mass one. Conversely, positivity of that tail means that the configuration has at least \(N\) entries. Since all entries are positive integers and their sum is \(N\), it has at most \(N\) entries. Hence it has exactly \(N\) entries, and every one of them is equal to one. This proves (15).

For completeness, the first time in (15) always exists. We establish the more general assertion
\[
r\leq N-k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{there is a time \(t\) with }Q_N(t,k)\geq r. \tag{16}
\]
The auxiliary observation is that
\[
r+1\leq Q_N(t,k)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
r\leq Q_N(t+r,k+1). \tag{17}
\]
This follows by induction on \(r\). The case \(r=0\) is trivial. For the induction step, the induction hypothesis supplies a lower bound at index \(k+1\) after \(r\) steps, while time monotonicity preserves the original lower bound at index \(k\). Formula (2) then shows that one further averaging step gives the required next integer lower bound.

We prove (16) by induction on \(k\). At \(k=0\), \(Q_N(t,0)=N\), so time zero works. To pass from \(k\) to \(k+1\), the assertion is trivial when \(r=0\). If \(r>0\) and \(r\leq N-(k+1)\), then \(r+1\leq N-k\). By the induction hypothesis, at some time the entry at index \(k\) is at least \(r+1\); applying (17) eventually makes the entry at index \(k+1\) at least \(r\). This proves (16).

Taking \(k=N-1\) and \(r=1\) in (16), and then using (15), shows that a stable time exists. Let
\[
T(N)=\min\{t:S_N(t)=(1,\ldots,1)\}.
\]
This is exactly the sequence value \(a(N)\) for \(N>0\). By (9) and (15), once the automaton is stable it remains stable. By the definition of the minimum, it is not stable at any time smaller than \(T(N)\).

We can now compare consecutive stabilization times. First consider the small initial value \(N=1\). The configuration \([1]\) is already stable, so
\[
T(1)=0.
\]
For mass two, one step changes \([2]\) to \([1,1]\), whereas \([2]\) is not initially stable. Thus
\[
T(2)=1=T(1)+1.
\]

Now let \(N\geq2\), and write
\[
t=T(N).
\]
By stability and (15),
\[
Q_N(t,N-1)\geq1. \tag{18}
\]
Apply the diagonal comparison (11) with \(k=N-2\). Since \((N-2)+1=N-1\), (18) gives
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,N-2)\geq3. \tag{19}
\]
Monotonicity in the initial mass, (7), also gives
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,N-1)\geq1. \tag{20}
\]
Using the recurrence (2), (19) and (20) imply
\[
Q_{N+1}(t+1,N-1)
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{Q_{N+1}(t,N-2)+Q_{N+1}(t,N-1)}2
\right\rfloor
\geq2. \tag{21}
\]
One more use of (2), now moving from index \(N-1\) to index \(N\), yields
\[
Q_{N+1}(t+2,N)
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{Q_{N+1}(t+1,N-1)+Q_{N+1}(t+1,N)}2
\right\rfloor
\geq1, \tag{22}
\]
because the first summand is at least two and the second is nonnegative. By the stability criterion (15), with total mass \(N+1\), (22) says that the mass-\(N+1\) automaton is stable by time \(t+2\). Therefore
\[
T(N+1)\leq t+2. \tag{23}
\]

It remains to prove that it cannot already be stable at time \(t\). Suppose to the contrary that it were. Then (15) would give
\[
Q_{N+1}(t,N)>0. \tag{24}
\]
If \(t=0\), this is impossible because every positive-index entry of the initial row is zero. If \(t=s+1\), apply the time-shifted comparison (14) with \(k=N-1\). From (24) we obtain
\[
Q_N(s,N-1)>0.
\]
By (15), the mass-\(N\) automaton was already stable at time \(s<t=T(N)\), contradicting the minimality of \(T(N)\). Hence the mass-\(N+1\) automaton is not stable at time \(t\).

If one had \(T(N+1)\leq t\), persistence of stability would make it stable at time \(t\), which we have just ruled out. Consequently
\[
t<T(N+1). \tag{25}
\]
Combining (23) and (25), and using integrality, leaves exactly two possibilities:
\[
T(N+1)=t+1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
T(N+1)=t+2.
\]
Since \(t=T(N)\), this says
\[
T(N+1)=T(N)+1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
T(N+1)=T(N)+2.
\]
The separately handled case \(N=1\) satisfies the same conclusion. Finally, \(a(N)=T(N)\) by the definition of the OEIS sequence as the first stabilization time. Therefore, for every integer \(N\geq1\),
\[
a(N+1)-a(N)\in\{1,2\},
\]
or equivalently
\[
a(N+1)=a(N)+1\quad\text{or}\quad a(N+1)=a(N)+2.
\]
This is the desired result.
